## This portfolio website and AI chatbot

Source: [This portfolio website and AI chatbot](https://arturoarias.me/projects/this-portfolio.html)

Website  AI / LLM  HTML  CSS  JavaScript  Cloudflare Workers  Cloudflare Workers AI  LLM  RAG  REST API  Cloudflare KV  Google Apps Script  GitHub Pages

A static ePortfolio built from scratch with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, paired with an AI chat assistant powered by a Cloudflare Workers API, a RAG pipeline over Cloudflare KV, and Llama 3.1 8B running on Cloudflare Workers AI.

Year

2026

Context/Client

Personal project

Topic/Field/Industry

Web development

[GitHub](https://github.com/arturoarias12)

The portfolio you are reading right now.

0

External framework dependencies — pure HTML, CSS, JS

12

Project case studies documented

20

RAG documents in Cloudflare KV powering the AI assistant

2

Themes — light and dark, persisted via localStorage

### Why build it from scratch?

Most portfolio templates come with a framework you did not choose, opinions you did not form, and constraints you have to fight. Building from scratch meant every layout decision, every color token, and every interaction was deliberate.

The goal was not to demonstrate that I can use a site builder. The goal was to produce a site that reflects how I actually think about design and engineering — precise, readable, fast, and maintainable by one person.

### Design decisions

#### CSS custom properties as the design system

All colors, radii, spacing units, and transition timings live in `:root` as CSS variables. Dark mode is implemented by swapping the values at the `[data-theme="dark"]` selector level — no JavaScript class toggling, no duplicated style blocks.

css

```
:root {
--primary: rgb(0, 0, 190);
--bg: #ffffff;
--text: #0a0a3a;
--text-muted: #5f5e5a;
}
[data-theme="dark"] {
--primary: rgb(41, 98, 255);
--bg: #050510;
--text: #e8e8f5;
--text-muted: #b0bcdd;
}
```

#### Sticky avatar navbar

The navbar is sticky with a frosted-glass background (`backdrop-filter: blur`), collapses to a hamburger at 820px, and uses a circular avatar image as the brand mark. All scroll-linked behaviors use a single `scroll` event listener with `passive: true`.

#### Projects system

Projects are defined in a single `projects-data.js` file as a plain JavaScript array. The listing page (`projects.html`) reads this array and renders cards dynamically, with client-side search, category filters, tag filters, sort, and grid/list view toggle — no server, no build step, no framework.

### Google Apps Script contact form

The contact form posts to a Google Apps Script endpoint using `fetch` with `Content-Type: text/plain` (required to avoid a preflight CORS request). The script reads the JSON payload, validates it, and emails the submission to my inbox. A honeypot field is included to block naive bots.

javascript

```
fetch(SCRIPT_URL, {
method: 'POST',
headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' },
body: JSON.stringify({ name, email, message })
})
.then(r => r.json())
.then(data => {
if (data.result === 'success') showSuccess();
else showError();
});
```

### AI chat assistant

Every page on the site includes a floating AI chat assistant that answers questions about Arturo's background, projects, experience, and skills. The widget is a self-contained vanilla JavaScript IIFE injected via a shared script. The intelligence lives entirely server-side in a Cloudflare Worker.

#### Architecture

The frontend sends a single `{ message }` field to the Worker API. The Worker performs RAG retrieval, builds the prompt, calls the LLM, and returns `{ answer }`. No API keys or system prompts are exposed to the browser.

architecture

```
Browser widget
POST { message }
↓
Cloudflare Worker  ←  WAF rate limiting
1. Input validation
2. Load index.json from KV → score docs → fetch top matches
3. Build system prompt + RAG context (encrypted env variable)
↓
Cloudflare Workers AI — Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (fp8-fast)
↓
{ answer }
↓
Browser widget renders markdown response
```

#### RAG pipeline (Cloudflare KV)

The knowledge base is 20 Markdown files covering every section of the site: about, experience, education, skills, certifications, all 12 projects, blog, and contact. Each file is stored as an individual entry in a Cloudflare KV namespace. An `index.json` maps filenames to titles and keyword arrays.

For each request the Worker loads the index, scores each document against the query using title and keyword overlap, fetches the top matching documents from KV, and injects their content into the system prompt. This keeps the LLM grounded in site-specific facts without fine-tuning the model.

#### LLM inference via Cloudflare Workers AI

The language model runs on Cloudflare's global edge inference infrastructure through the `env.AI` binding. No external API key is required. The system prompt is stored as an encrypted Cloudflare environment variable — it never appears in source code or version control.

javascript

```
const ai = await env.AI.run('@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct-fp8-fast', {
messages: [
{ role: 'system', content: systemPrompt + ragContext },
{ role: 'user',   content: message },
],
max_tokens: 512,
temperature: 0.5,
});
return Response.json({ answer: ai.response });
```

#### Security and rate limiting

Rate limiting is enforced at the Cloudflare WAF level, with a block action applied per IP on excess requests. The Worker additionally validates HTTP method, Content-Type, JSON structure, message length, and message count before any inference call is made. The system prompt includes explicit instructions against prompt injection, jailbreaking, and out-of-scope requests.

Custom domain

The chatbot API is served from a dedicated Cloudflare custom subdomain wired to the Worker. The portfolio itself is hosted on GitHub Pages under `arturoarias.me`, managed through Cloudflare DNS.

### Tools & tech

Frontend

HTML5 CSS3 Vanilla JS

AI / LLM

Cloudflare Workers AI Llama 3.1 8B Instruct RAG Prompt Engineering

Backend / API

Cloudflare Workers REST API Google Apps Script

Storage

Cloudflare KV

Infrastructure

Cloudflare WAF Cloudflare DNS GitHub Pages

Typography

Inter JetBrains Mono

### Reflections

The hardest part was not the code — it was the copy. Every word on this site required deciding what to say and what to leave out. Building the design system took an afternoon; editing the About page took three days.

If I were starting over: I would define the CSS token system before writing a single HTML element. I refactored the color tokens twice after painting myself into a dark-mode corner with hard-coded values.

## Perspectives on Three AI Ecosystems: From "Best Model" to "Best Match"

Source: [Perspectives on Three AI Ecosystems: From "Best Model" to "Best Match"](https://arturoarias.me/blog/ai-ecosystems.html)

[Home](https://arturoarias.me/index.html) /  [Insights](https://arturoarias.me/blog.html) /  Perspectives on Three AI Ecosystems

Artificial Intelligence  LLM  Agentic AI  Productivity  Personal

Using three ecosystems (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) side by side changed the question for me from "Which model is the best?" to "Which kind of collaboration does this task need?"

AA Arturo Arias    August 21, 2026   5 min read

During the past four months, I have been deliberately using ChatGPT and Codex, Claude and Claude Code, and Gemini side by side.

In summary, the main insight is: **the most useful AI is not always the one that gives the "best" answer. Sometimes, it is the one whose behavior best matches how you want to work.**

Before this experiment, I mostly used only ChatGPT for almost everything; but after repeatedly hearing from colleagues and classmates that I was missing out on Claude (and seeing what Google was building around Gemini and its broader ecosystem), I decided to subscribe to all three so I could experience each one firsthand. The decision was also reinforced by my growing recognition that, given the pace at which these models are evolving, maintaining practical familiarity requires continuous hands-on exposure to their capabilities.

I used them across ordinary work (on my own personal projects): drafting and refining emails, summarizing information, generating images, researching, automating repetitive tasks, writing code, and working directly inside larger codebases through coding agents.

What follows in this blog post is purely my experience of how these tools fit into my workflows. It is not a technical benchmark, an academic evaluation, or an attempt to decide which company has the "best" model. These products evolve too quickly for a temporary performance gap to be the most interesting comparison. Their working styles have been much more useful to examine.

### OpenAI: an amplifier of my thinking

In my experience, ChatGPT and Codex feel the closest to an **amplifier of my own thinking**.

When I have a clear idea of what I want, I can give precise instructions and generally expect the result to remain closely aligned with them. That is particularly valuable in areas where I already have expertise.

Python is a good example. If I already understand the architecture, implementation, and trade-offs I want, my main reason for using AI is **efficiency**: execute the plan, reduce repetitive work, generate or modify files, and help me move faster without giving up control of the direction.

Nevertheless, that efficiency comes with a trade-off: if I omit something important in my instructions, that omission can carry into the result. The system can accelerate execution and testing, but the underlying thinking, judgment, and details still need to come from me.

That interaction style works extremely well for me when **precision, alignment, and control are the priority**.

### Anthropic: a more exploratory collaborator

By comparison, my experience with Claude has felt different.

Initially, I hesitated to subscribe because of my uncertainty about whether another subscription would be worthwhile. Nonetheless, I eventually tried it after receiving recommendations that it could often reach strong results with fewer iterations (which meant less back-and-forth and less token usage). My experience ended up being more nuanced than that.

I did not consistently find that Claude required substantially fewer prompts than Codex. What I noticed was more interesting: **the two often approach the same task differently.**

Claude frequently feels more willing to expand beyond the literal request—proposing alternatives, surfacing considerations I did not mention, or introducing ideas that might improve the overall solution.

When I already know exactly what I want, that extra initiative is not always what I need. In contrast, when I am entering a less familiar area, it becomes very valuable.

In those situations, I am not only automating manual work: I am also accelerating part of the learning and information-processing process. Claude can expose me to possibilities I might not have considered, giving me more material to evaluate while I develop my own understanding (without me having to explicitly ask for it).

Through experimentation, I found that a particularly effective workflow is to let the tools **collaborate conceptually**. For instance, Codex can take ownership of an implementation and make changes across a project[1](https://arturoarias.me/blog/ai-ecosystems.html#editorial-note), while Claude serves as a reviewer or QA partner, challenging decisions, identifying potential issues, and suggesting improvements. The results have been consistently strong enough that this has become a workflow I now use quite often.

### Google: the productivity advantage of integration

Gemini has occupied another interesting position in my toolkit.

For some of the more complex tasks in the particular workflows I have attempted, I have tended to reach first for ChatGPT (and Codex) or Claude. Yet, I deliberately routed work to Gemini, specifically the high-frequency tasks already embedded in Google's ecosystem. For example, I used Gemini in Chrome to extract data directly from websites and summarize content without leaving the page, to refactor code quickly inside Google Colab, and to build automations that pull data from Drive and write it into other files without requiring additional integrations or setup[2](https://arturoarias.me/blog/ai-ecosystems.html#editorial-note). Judged on that kind of work, Gemini’s biggest strength is not a capability gap at all. It is **where the model lives**.

The wider set of tools adds another dimension to the experience. Image and video generation, along with models such as Lyria for music generation, expand what can be created within Google's ecosystem.[2](https://arturoarias.me/blog/ai-ecosystems.html#editorial-note)

For many everyday tasks, convenience and integration can matter just as much as maximum capability on a difficult, isolated prompt.

### Assigning roles instead of choosing a winner

After using all three, I have become less interested in asking:

Asking less

Which AI model is the best?

And much more interested in asking:

Asking more

Which AI behavior is best for this particular task?

**Sometimes I want precise execution of what I asked for.** I know the direction and want the system to help me move faster.

**Sometimes I want productive challenge.** I need alternatives, questions, and possibilities I have not yet considered.

**Sometimes I want contextual convenience.** The biggest gain comes from having AI integrated directly into the tools where the work already happens.

The most powerful workflow may not come from choosing one ecosystem at all: it may come from **learning how to combine them according to their strengths and according to our own knowledge, preferences, and working style.**

What approach have you found works best for you? If you regularly use ChatGPT and Codex, Claude and Claude Code, Gemini, or a combination of them, have you also noticed differences in how they work with you, beyond simply comparing the quality of their outputs?[3](https://arturoarias.me/blog/ai-ecosystems.html#editorial-note)

1 [OpenAI, Codex overview](https://developers.openai.com/codex/).
2 Google, [Gemini in Chrome](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16283624); [Gemini in Google Drive](https://workspace.google.com/intl/en/products/drive/ai/); [Google Colab](https://developers.google.com/colab); [Google DeepMind, generative-model cards for image, music, and video generation](https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/).
3 **Editorial note:** The ideas, experiences, comparisons, and conclusions in this article are my own. I used ChatGPT to help refine the wording and structure of the final draft.

### Continue the conversation

Have you developed your own way of combining these tools, or do you approach them differently? I would be interested to hear your perspective.

[aaarias@andrew.cmu.edu](mailto:aaarias@andrew.cmu.edu)

## Hello, world: this site is live

Source: [Hello, world: this site is live](https://arturoarias.me/blog/welcome.html)

[Home](https://arturoarias.me/index.html) /  [Insights](https://arturoarias.me/blog.html) /  Hello, world

Personal  Web Development

A first entry on why I built this place, what it is for, and what I hope to do with it.

AA  Arturo Arias     May 21, 2026   3 min read

This is my first entry here, and it feels right to use it to explain what this place actually is.

I have wanted a proper personal website for a long time. The first version I built was years ago, using Django and Python. It worked, but it was more complex than it needed to be, and I eventually stopped maintaining it. This version is different: static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, no framework, no backend. It is purpose-built as an ePortfolio, and it is designed to live on GitHub Pages indefinitely without a running server. I used Claude Design (preview) as an aid throughout the process, which accelerated the work considerably and let me focus on decisions rather than boilerplate.

### Why not just a résumé?

A résumé is, by nature, compressed. It lists outcomes, not process. It names tools, not reasoning. It has to fit on one or two pages, which means almost everything that makes the work interesting gets cut.

There is also a structural problem: résumés submitted online are frequently filtered by applicant tracking systems before a human ever reads them. That process rewards keyword density and formatting compliance, not the quality of the underlying work. This site is built for the reviewer who reaches it directly. The [projects section](https://arturoarias.me/index.html#projects) covers BI and data engineering work, Python automation, machine learning experiments, and database systems, each with enough context to show the thinking behind it. A hiring manager or recruiter who wants to understand how I approach a problem can find the actual reasoning here, not just the outcome.

This site has more room. The projects section can show the actual approach, not just the result. The skills page can reflect real depth instead of a comma-separated list of keywords. And this blog is a place for things that do not belong anywhere else: research interests, observations from real work, reflections on topics like AI, data systems, communication, and the softer dimensions of technical roles.

There is also a practical side. A lot of my best work does not live on GitHub. Dashboards, client-facing reports, private analytics pipelines, case studies built inside company systems. None of that has a public URL. A portfolio like this gives that work a home, even if the full detail has to stay confidential.

### What comes next

Some posts here will be long-form. Some will be brief field notes. Topics will range across data engineering, BI, AI, and the occasional piece on communication or team dynamics. I do not have a strict publishing schedule, but I expect to write regularly now that the infrastructure is in place.

If you are visiting because you found the link on LinkedIn or in a résumé: Welcome! I hope the experience is clean and the content is worth your time.

If something here sparked a thought or question, feel free to [reach out](https://arturoarias.me/index.html#contact).

### Get in touch

Have a question, a project idea, or just want to connect? I would love to hear from you.
